ground_truth.description: The lock() function intends to lock the user's entire approved balance, but this will fail for the most common case: Most users give contracts they interact with an unlimited allowance by setting it to type(uint256).max. The _incomingTokenBalance() function at line 32 returns just 'erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this))' which would be type(uint256).max for unlimited approvals. The lock() function then attempts to transfer this impossible amount.
ground_truth.root_cause: The lock() function intends to lock the user's entire approved balance, but this will fail for the most common case: Most users give contracts they interact with an unlimited allowance by setting it to type(uint256).max. The _incomingTokenBalance() function at line 32 returns just 'erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this))' which would be type(uint256).max for unlimited approvals. The lock() function then attempts to transfer this impossible amount.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. User approves LockManager with unlimited allowance: approve(lockManager, type(uint256).max).
2. User calls lock() without specifying an amount.
3. _incomingTokenBalance() returns type(uint256).max.
4. _doLockTransfer attempts to transfer type(uint256).max tokens.
5. Transaction reverts because user doesn't have that many tokens.
6. User cannot use the standard lock() function.
ground_truth.fix_description: Have _incomingTokenBalance() return either the actual balance or the allowance depending on whichever is smallest: 'return (allowance >= balance) ? balance : allowance;'

vulnerabilities.explanation: The _incomingTokenBalance() function returns only the allowance amount (erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this))) without considering the user's actual token balance. When users grant unlimited approval (type(uint256).max), which is the most common pattern for DeFi interactions, this function returns type(uint256).max. The lock() function in LockManagerBase likely uses this value to determine how many tokens to transfer when no explicit amount is specified. Since no user actually holds type(uint256).max tokens, the subsequent transferFrom call in _doLockTransfer will always revert for users with unlimited approvals who don't specify an explicit lock amount.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. User wants to lock tokens in the LockManager. 2. User approves LockManagerERC20 with unlimited allowance: erc20Token.approve(lockManager, type(uint256).max). 3. User calls lock() without specifying an amount, expecting to lock their entire balance. 4. _incomingTokenBalance() returns type(uint256).max (the allowance). 5. _doLockTransfer attempts to call transferFrom for type(uint256).max tokens. 6. Transaction reverts because user doesn't have that many tokens. 7. Users with unlimited approvals cannot use the default lock functionality and must always specify explicit amounts.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Modify _incomingTokenBalance() to return the minimum of the user's actual balance and their allowance: function _incomingTokenBalance() internal view virtual override returns (uint256) { uint256 allowance = erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this)); uint256 balance = erc20Token.balanceOf(msg.sender); return allowance >= balance ? balance : allowance; }

prediction.overall_explanation: The LockManagerERC20 contract contains a logic error in the _incomingTokenBalance() function. This function is designed to determine how many tokens a user can lock when they don't specify an explicit amount. However, it only checks the allowance without considering the user's actual token balance. Since the standard practice in DeFi is to grant unlimited approvals (type(uint256).max), this function will return an impossibly large value for most users. When the lock mechanism attempts to transfer this amount, the transaction will fail because no user holds that many tokens. This effectively breaks the default lock functionality for the majority of users who follow standard approval patterns, forcing them to always specify explicit amounts or use limited approvals.
